This patient's ECG rhythm strip shows normal sinus rhythm; close inspection reveals that the height of the QRS complexes alternates with each cycle (noticeable in precordial lead V1), a finding known as electrical alternans. Electrical alternans is a specific but poorly sensitive (often not present) finding for pericardial effusion with cardiac tamponade; it results from the heart changing position within the fluid-filled pericardial sac with each heartbeat. Low-voltage QRS complexes (eg, <10 mm in precordial leads), as seen in this patient, are a moderately sensitive and moderately specific finding for cardiac tamponade that results from attenuation of cardiac electrical signals by fluid within the pericardial sac.

Viral infection is a common cause of acute pericarditis, which can be complicated by pericardial effusion. This patient has likely experienced slow accumulation of fluid within the pericardial sac, leading to progressive symptoms of weakness, dyspnea, and chest discomfort. Eventually, the fluid compresses the relatively low-pressure right-sided heart chambers and restricts diastolic filling, leading to subacute tamponade. With the right-sided heart chambers unable to fill, less blood is delivered to the left side of the heart and cardiac output drops, leading to hypotension and associated symptoms (eg, lightheadedness, syncope). Treatment requires emergency pericardiocentesis to relieve pericardial pressure and restore blood flow through the chambers of the heart.
educationalObjective: Electrical alternans and low-voltage QRS complexes on ECG are characteristic findings of pericardial effusion with cardiac tamponade. Emergency pericardiocentesis is required to relieve pericardial pressure and restore cardiac output.

stem: A 65-year-old man comes to the physician for fatigue, poor appetite, and lower-leg swelling. Past medical history is significant for hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic cough, chest infections, and lower-extremity peripheral artery disease. The patient has a 40-pack-year smoking history. He does not use alcohol or illicit drugs. Physical examination shows a barrel-shaped chest, with bilateral scattered wheezing on auscultation. The patient's abdomen is distended, and the liver edge is palpated 4 cm below the right costal margin. There is 2+ pitting edema and dilated, tortuous superficial veins over both lower extremities. Manual pressure on the abdomen causes persistent distension of the jugular veins. His serum sodium level is 135 mEq/L, and creatinine is 1.2 mg/dL. An abnormality of which of the following is most likely the cause of this patient's edema?

explanations.A: Increased portal venous resistance (portal hypertension) is seen in the setting of hepatic cirrhosis or extrahepatic portal vein thrombosis. Chronic liver disease is associated with stigmata such as palmar erythema, spider angiomata, caput medusae, and gynecomastia. Complications of cirrhosis with portal hypertension include ascites, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, and variceal bleeding.
explanations.B: This patient's clinical findings (long-term tobacco use, chronic cough, barrel-shaped chest, elevated jugular venous pressure, and enlarged liver) are consistent with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) with cor pulmonale, which is caused by pulmonary hypertension (elevated pulmonary artery systolic pressure >25 mm Hg).
explanations.C: The pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP) is an estimation of left ventricular end-diastolic pressure, and is elevated in patients with left ventricular systolic and/or diastolic dysfunction. Patients with elevated PCWP typically have signs of pulmonary edema on lung auscultation.
explanations.D: Hypoalbuminemia may occur due to decreased hepatic synthesis (cirrhosis) or increased urinary or gastrointestinal protein loss (ie, nephrotic syndrome, protein-losing enteropathy). Nephrotic syndrome typically presents with periorbital and pedal edema that may progress to generalized edema (anasarca), ascites, and pleural effusions. This patient does not have anasarca or facial edema; he also does not have stigmata of chronic liver disease or diarrhea (to suggest enteropathy).
explanations.E: Hypoalbuminemia may occur due to increased urinary protein loss (nephrotic syndrome), which typically presents with periorbital and pedal edema that may progress to generalized edema (anasarca), ascites, and pleural effusions.

generalExplanation:
This patient's clinical findings—long-term tobacco use, chronic cough, barrel-shaped chest, elevated jugular venous pressure, and enlarged liver—are consistent with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) with cor pulmonale. Cor pulmonale refers to impaired function of the right ventricle caused by pulmonary hypertension that occurs due to underlying diseases of the lungs (COPD, interstitial lung disease), pulmonary vasculature (idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension), or obstructive sleep apnea. By convention, right ventricular dysfunction due to left heart disease or congenital heart disease is not considered cor pulmonale.

Patients with cor pulmonale typically present with exertional symptoms (eg, dyspnea, angina, syncope), anorexia or abdominal pain (due to hepatic congestion), and peripheral edema. Physical examination may show a loud P2 (pulmonic component of 2nd heart sound) and a right ventricular 3rd heart sound, tricuspid regurgitation murmur (holosystolic at the left lower sternal border, augments with inspiration), elevated jugular venous pressure with hepatojugular reflux, hepatomegaly with pulsatile liver, and occasionally ascites or pleural effusion. The diagnosis of cor pulmonale is based primarily on clinical features and echocardiographic findings (eg, right ventricular hypertrophy, tricuspid regurgitation with right atrial enlargement). If necessary, definitive diagnosis can be made using right heart catheterization showing elevated pulmonary artery systolic pressure (>25 mm Hg).
educationalObjective: Cor pulmonale is impaired function of the right ventricle due to pulmonary hypertension that usually occurs due to chronic lung disease. Signs of right ventricular failure include elevated jugular venous pressure, right ventricular 3rd heart sound, tricuspid regurgitation murmur, hepatomegaly, and peripheral edema.

stem: A 72-year-old man comes to the emergency department due to severe left lower leg pain that began as a tingling sensation several hours ago but has since become increasingly painful. Medical history is significant for hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, and osteoarthritis. The patient has a 45-pack-year smoking history. Blood pressure is 142/80 mm Hg, and pulse is 112/min and irregular. On physical examination, the left lower extremity skin appears mottled and is cool to the touch. The distal pulses of the left leg are not palpable. There is a right carotid bruit. Which of the following medications could have best prevented this patient's acute condition?

explanations.A: Apixaban is a non-vitamin K antagonist oral anticoagulant (NOAC) that directly inhibits factor Xa, preventing it from cleaving prothrombin to thrombin. The NOACs (eg, apixaban, dabigatran, rivaroxaban, edoxaban) significantly reduce systemic embolization risk with similar or superior efficacy as warfarin but with decreased risk of severe bleeding (eg, hemorrhagic stroke) and no need for routine INR testing.
explanations.B: In contrast, antiplatelet therapy with aspirin or a combination of aspirin and clopidogrel is significantly less effective in reducing thromboembolic risk compared with anticoagulant therapy with NOACs or warfarin.
explanations.C: Cilostazol is a phosphodiesterase inhibitor occasionally used for symptomatic management of patients with intermittent claudication. Although cilostazol also suppresses platelet aggregation, it is not indicated for primary thromboembolic event prevention in patients with AF.
explanations.D: In contrast, antiplatelet therapy with aspirin or a combination of aspirin and clopidogrel is significantly less effective in reducing thromboembolic risk compared with anticoagulant therapy with NOACs or warfarin.
explanations.E: Calcium channel blockers (eg, diltiazem) and beta blockers (eg, metoprolol) are used for heart rate control in patients with AF. Rate control helps manage symptoms and avoid hemodynamic instability from rapid ventricular response; however, unlike anticoagulation, it does not prevent thromboembolic events.
explanations.F: Calcium channel blockers (eg, diltiazem) and beta blockers (eg, metoprolol) are used for heart rate control in patients with AF. Rate control helps manage symptoms and avoid hemodynamic instability from rapid ventricular response; however, unlike anticoagulation, it does not prevent thromboembolic events.

generalExplanation:
This patient with acute lower extremity pain, paresthesia, and pulselessness has acute limb ischemia. Given the patient's history of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation (AF) and irregular pulse on examination, the most likely cause is embolism of a left atrial thrombus, which might have been prevented by appropriate anticoagulation therapy.

Current guidelines recommend the use of the CHA2DS2-VASc score for thromboembolic risk assessment in patients with AF. Patients with a CHA2DS2-VASc score >=2, such as this patient (score = 3: hypertension, diabetes mellitus, age 65-74), are at high risk of thromboembolic events and should be managed with anticoagulation therapy. In these patients, the benefit of lowered embolization risk outweighs the risk of bleeding (eg, intracranial hemorrhage).

Apixaban is a non-vitamin K antagonist oral anticoagulant (NOAC) that directly inhibits factor Xa, preventing it from cleaving prothrombin to thrombin. The NOACs (eg, apixaban, dabigatran, rivaroxaban, edoxaban) significantly reduce systemic embolization risk with similar or superior efficacy as warfarin but with decreased risk of severe bleeding (eg, hemorrhagic stroke) and no need for routine INR testing.
educationalObjective: Anticoagulation agents, such as non-vitamin K antagonist oral anticoagulants (eg, apixaban) and warfarin, should be used to reduce the risk of systemic thromboembolism in patients with atrial fibrillation and a high risk of thromboembolic events (ie, CHA2DS2-VASc score >=2).

stem: A 59-year-old man comes to the emergency department due to chest pain beginning 2 hours ago and profuse sweating 1 hour ago. He feels weak. Past medical history includes type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypercholesterolemia. The patient's medications include metformin, glipizide, and simvastatin. Blood pressure is 165/98 mm Hg in the right arm and 160/90 mm Hg in the left, pulse is 78/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. He appears mildly uncomfortable. Lungs are clear to auscultation. His ECG is shown in exhibit. Which of the following is the best next step in management of this patient?

options.A: Aspirin, cardiac enzyme levels, and observation in the intensive care unit
options.B: Aspirin, heparin infusion, and admission to the telemetry floor
options.E: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs as needed for pain

explanations.A: Patients with acute STEMI should go directly to coronary angiography from the emergency department and are usually managed in an intensive care unit rather than a standard telemetry unit following urgent coronary intervention.
explanations.B: Patients with acute STEMI should go directly to coronary angiography from the emergency department and are usually managed in an intensive care unit rather than a standard telemetry unit following urgent coronary intervention.

explanations.D: Acute, type A aortic dissection (ascending aortic dissection) can occasionally cause occlusion of the right coronary artery by the dissection flap, leading to inferior MI. These patients are typically hypotensive. More commonly, patients with aortic dissection have sharp or tearing chest or back pain and nonspecific ECG changes. Patients with pulmonary embolism usually have dyspnea, tachypnea, tachycardia, and hypoxia.
explanations.E: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs are used in the management of acute pericarditis. Patients typically have sharp and pleuritic chest pain that is worse with deep inspiration or when supine and relieved with sitting up and leaning forward. ECGs classically show diffuse ST-segment elevation and PR-segment depression in the limb and left precordial leads.

generalExplanation:
This patient's clinical features and ECG findings (ST-segment elevation in leads I, aVL, and V2-V6 with reciprocal ST-segment depression in leads II, III, and aVF) suggest acute anterolateral ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) due to left anterior descending artery occlusion. In patients with a typical presentation, STEMI can be diagnosed even without cardiac biomarkers (can be normal early on). Immediate coronary reperfusion therapy is indicated following initial stabilization measures, which include: oxygen, full-dose aspirin (chewed to enter the bloodstream quickly), platelet P2Y12 receptor blocker (eg, clopidogrel, ticagrelor), nitroglycerin (relieves ischemic pain; morphine if nitroglycerin is inadequate), beta blocker, and anticoagulation (ie, heparin).

Prompt coronary reperfusion with primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) or fibrinolytic therapy (eg, alteplase) restores blood flow, limits myocardial damage, and reduces mortality. Current guidelines recommend primary PCI for patients with acute STEMI as follows:
- Within 12 hours of symptom onset AND
- Within 90 minutes from first medical contact to device time at a PCI-capable facility OR
- Within 120 minutes from first medical contact to device time at a non-PCI-capable facility (to allow time for transport to a PCI-capable facility)

Multiple randomized trials have shown lower rates of recurrent MI and intracranial hemorrhage, and improved survival with primary PCI compared to fibrinolytic therapy. This patient who is within 12 hours of symptom onset (onset 2 hours ago) and at a PCI-capable facility should ideally undergo PCI within 90 minutes of first medical contact. Fibrinolysis is recommended for STEMI patients arriving within 12 hours of symptom onset who cannot undergo PCI (eg, PCI is not available within the recommended time frame).
educationalObjective: Primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) is recommended within 90 minutes for acute, ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). Additional stabilization measures include oxygen, full-dose aspirin, platelet P2Y12 receptor blockers, nitroglycerin, beta blockers, and anticoagulation. Fibrinolysis may be administered within 12 hours of symptom onset for STEMI patients who cannot undergo PCI but is associated with higher rates of recurrent myocardial infarction, intracranial hemorrhage, and mortality compared to PCI.

stem: A 45-year-old man comes to the office due to several abnormal blood pressure readings over the past year. He also has had fatigue, which he attributes to stress at work. The patient is a carpenter, and his diet consists primarily of fast food several times a day because he is busy with worksite jobs. He wakes up several times at night and occasionally finds it difficult to fall back asleep. He has had no chest pain, shortness of breath, light-headedness, or syncope. Family history is negative for hypertension, stroke, and early-onset coronary artery disease. The patient drinks 2 beers a day on weekends. Blood pressure is 151/90 mm Hg on the right arm and 159/95 mm Hg on the left. Repeat blood pressure on the left arm is 158/94 mm Hg. Pulse is 78/min and regular. BMI is 32 kg/m2. Physical examination is unremarkable. ECG shows normal sinus rhythm with no abnormalities. Serum chemistry panel and TSH are within normal limits. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's hypertension?

explanations.A: Heavy drinking (>=5 drinks in a single sitting) can cause hypertension. However, intermittent, moderate intake (<=1 drink a day for women, <=2 for men) does not seem to significantly increase risk. This patient drinks only 2 beers daily on weekends; it is unlikely that alcohol caused his hypertension.
explanations.B: Generalized anxiety disorder can increase the risk of hypertension, but this patient's nocturnal awakenings, daytime fatigue, and underlying obesity are more suggestive of OSA.
explanations.C: This patient with hypertension has obesity, nocturnal awakenings, and daytime fatigue, consistent with obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). Because nighttime apneic episodes trigger a strong catecholamine response, many (~50%) patients with OSA develop secondary hypertension.
explanations.D: Primary hyperaldosteronism should be suspected in patients with hypertension associated with hypokalemia (either at baseline or after initiation of low-dose diuretic therapy). Disrupted sleep is not a typical feature.
explanations.E: Renovascular hypertension is generally suspected in those with widespread atherosclerosis, abdominal bruit, new-onset hypertension at an advanced age, acute kidney injury after initiation of an ACE inhibitor, or recurrent flash pulmonary edema/resistant heart failure.

generalExplanation:
This patient with hypertension has obesity, nocturnal awakenings, and daytime fatigue, consistent with obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). Men with obesity are at greatest risk. In OSA, upper airway obstruction (due to pharyngeal muscle relaxation during sleep) causes progressive hypoxia and hypercapnia until chemoreceptors in the carotid body and brainstem trigger arousal, which restores pharyngeal tone. Manifestations usually include nocturnal awakenings, daytime fatigue, and reports of loud snoring and apneic episodes from sleeping partners. Patients commonly report difficulty maintaining or falling back to sleep.

Because nighttime apneic episodes trigger a strong catecholamine response, many (~50%) patients with OSA develop secondary hypertension. Although the hypertension is often recalcitrant to antihypertensive medications, it generally improves or resolves with treatment of the underlying OSA (eg, nighttime continuous positive airway pressure). Other cardiovascular conditions frequently triggered by OSA include pulmonary hypertension, right-sided heart failure, coronary heart disease, and arrhythmias (eg, atrial fibrillation).
educationalObjective: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is a common cause of secondary hypertension due to the production of catecholamines during apneic episodes. The hypertension is often resistant to medications, but treatment of the underlying OSA (eg, nocturnal continuous positive airway pressure) often leads to resolution. Other cardiovascular complications of OSA include pulmonary hypertension, right-sided heart failure, coronary heart disease, and arrhythmias.

stem: A 6-year-old boy with congenital deafness is brought to the emergency department after fainting. He was running in his backyard when he suddenly fell to the ground and lost consciousness. The patient regained consciousness quickly and without confusion. The event was not associated with convulsions, tongue biting, or urinary incontinence. He has never had an episode like this before. The patient is developmentally normal and takes no medications. He underwent bilateral cochlear implantation at age 2 for sensorineural hearing loss. The patient had a brother who died during a swim meet at age 14. Blood pressure is normal. Cardiac examination reveals a regular heart rate and no murmurs. The remainder of the physical examination is unremarkable. Serum chemistry is normal. ECG is shown in the exhibit. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacologic treatment for this patient?

explanations.A: Ethosuximide is first-line treatment for absence seizures and levetiracetam is commonly used for treatment of other generalized seizures; however, this patient's episode of loss of consciousness (LOC) is most consistent with syncope. With absence seizures, LOC is not accompanied by loss of body tone (ie, collapse). With other generalized seizures, LOC is usually accompanied by jerking movements, tongue-biting, urinary incontinence, and/or postictal confusion.
explanations.B: Class IA antiarrhythmics (eg, quinidine) and class III antiarrhythmics (eg, ibutilide, sotalol) are contraindicated in LQTS because these drugs inhibit the repolarizing voltage-gated potassium channels and exacerbate the disease. Despite the beta-blocking properties of sotalol, the drug must be avoided in LQTS due to inhibitory effects on potassium channels.

With absence seizures, LOC is not accompanied by loss of body tone (ie, collapse). With other generalized seizures, LOC is usually accompanied by jerking movements, tongue-biting, urinary incontinence, and/or postictal confusion.
explanations.D: Beta blockers (class II antiarrhythmics) dampen sympathetic activity and shorten the QT interval at rapid heart rates to reduce the risk of syncope and death in patients with congenital LQTS; this benefit is most prominent with the nonselective beta blockers, propranolol and nadolol.
